title: You Might Not Need 50 Diffusion Steps — Ziv Ilan, Nvidia
talk_summary: Nvidia's Ziv Ilan explains three incremental optimizations for diffusion image/video models: quantization, caching (skip recomputing near-identical denoising steps), and step distillation (train a student to reach teacher quality in 4-8 steps instead of 50). The core transferable idea is a layered, incremental optimization stack where you start with the cheap low-risk win and escalate only if quality holds.

takeaways.what_they_do: They deploy optimizations in a fixed order (distillation, then quantization, then caching) and treat each as additive rather than mutually exclusive, stopping when quality is 'good enough'.

takeaways.technique: Skip recomputation when inputs barely change (caching)
takeaways.what_they_do: Compare consecutive denoising steps; if the change is below a threshold, reuse the prior computation instead of recomputing the whole thing, with chunk-level granularity.
takeaways.evidence_quote: if there's there was a minimal change or very small change between the denoising steps, it compares it and it understands, okay, now I don't need to um to recompute

takeaways.what_they_do: Every optimization is gated on maintaining output quality; they warn caching done wrong 'can have quite a significant impact on the quality' and require tuning thresholds and verifying.
takeaways.evidence_quote: Caching is something that if you don't do the right way, can have quite a significant impact on the quality of the image

takeaways.technique: Distill big-model behavior into a cheaper student
takeaways.what_they_do: Train a student model to match the teacher's output distribution (not its exact trajectory) so it reaches comparable quality in far fewer steps; distribution-based distillation is cited as the better-quality approach.
takeaways.evidence_quote: Training the model, the student model, to generate as good quality images or videos, but by using much less steps.
takeaways.numbers: 50 steps down to 4-8 steps, cited as 10x-200x performance improvement

takeaways.what_they_do: Post-training quantization (dynamic ranges computed on the fly) reduces memory so models run on lower-end GPUs, with modest speed gains; noted as less impactful for attention-heavy models.
takeaways.evidence_quote: the impact is both on the memory, okay? It will require less memory, which means you can run it on lower-end GPUs
